text: The hotel can _____ up to 200 guests.
note: A building or room accommodates people: it has space for them. Include and involve are about what is part of something; comprise means "consist of".

text: Many students find it difficult to _____ with the pressure of exams.
note: Cope with = deal successfully with something difficult. Handle and control take no "with": handle the pressure.

text: Sales have _____ sharply over the last two years, and the shop may have to close.
note: Decline = become less. (It can also mean say no politely: decline an invitation.) Refuse, reject and deny are only about saying no.

text: After hours of talks, the two sides finally reached a _____ that both could accept.
note: Reach a compromise = agree by each side giving up something. We make (not reach) a promise or a commitment.

text: _____ at the club's meetings has fallen since they were moved to Saturday.
note: Attendance = how many people go to something. Careful: assistance means help (Spanish asistencia can mean both).

text: He tried to _____ his disappointment, but everyone could see he was upset.
note: Conceal = hide, often a feeling or a fact. Store, keep and save are about things you put away, not feelings you hide.

text: It is _____ that you arrive on time for the interview, or they won't see you.
note: Crucial = extremely important. Severe, acute and intense describe how strong something bad is: a severe storm, acute pain.

text: The new airport is expected to _____ tourism in the region.
note: Boost = help something increase or improve. Rise and arise have no object; we heighten a feeling (heighten tension), not tourism.

text: He didn't want to become a _____ to his family when he got older.
note: Be a burden to someone = be a problem they have to take care of. Weight and load are about physical heaviness.

text: The minister refused to _____ on the rumours about her resignation.
note: Comment on something = give your opinion about it. Mention and say take no "on"; tell on someone means report their bad behaviour.

text: She had prepared well and passed the exam with _____.
note: With ease = easily, without difficulty. Comfort is about feeling physically relaxed; simplicity describes a thing, not how you do it.

text: I've decided to _____ on an evening course in Spanish.
note: Enrol on a course (British; American: enroll in). We sign up for a course, subscribe to a magazine and apply for a place.

text: The cost of the repairs could _____ £1,000.
note: Exceed = be more than an amount or limit. Overcome a problem, excel at something, overtake a car.

text: The singer rose to _____ after appearing on a TV talent show.
note: Rise to fame = become famous. A reputation is what people think of you, good or bad; you don't rise to it.

text: All our washing machines come with a two-year _____.
note: A guarantee = the maker's promise to repair or replace a product. Insurance is something you pay a company for.

text: My working hours are quite _____, so I can pick the children up from school.
note: Flexible hours = you can change when you work. Elastic and loose describe materials and clothes.

text: Under no _____ should you give your password to anyone.
note: Under no circumstances = never, in any situation (a fixed phrase, always plural). Note the word order after it: should you.

text: At only £10, this jacket is a real _____.
note: A bargain = something bought for much less than it is worth. A sale is an event; a discount is the money taken off the price.

text: Students have free _____ to the library's online resources.
note: Access to = the right or chance to use something. Entry and admission are about going into a place.

text: Please _____ attention to the safety instructions before the flight.
note: Pay attention to = listen or watch carefully. A fixed phrase: always pay.

text: Many people find it hard to _____ up smoking, even when they know it is harmful.
note: Give up = stop doing something. Take up smoking means start, which doesn't fit "even when they know it is harmful".

text: You should _____ advantage of the good weather and go for a walk.
note: Take advantage of = use a good situation. A fixed phrase: always take.

text: The concert was cancelled _____ to the heavy rain.
note: Due to = because of. We say because of (not because to), as a result of and for this reason.

text: The hotel was full, so we had no _____ but to stay at a campsite.
note: Have no choice but to = be forced to do something. A fixed phrase.

text: Studying abroad was a great _____ that taught me a lot about myself.
note: An experience = something that happens to you. An experiment is a scientific test; knowledge is uncountable (not "a knowledge").

text: He _____ me to bring an umbrella, but I forgot.
note: Remind someone to do something = tell them so they don't forget. You remember something yourself; nobody remembers you to do it.

text: The doctor _____ me to get more sleep.
note: Advise someone to do something. Suggest and recommend don't take this pattern: the doctor suggested (that) I get more sleep.

text: I'm afraid I can't _____ to go on holiday this year, because I haven't saved enough money.
note: Can afford to do something = have enough money for it. We pay for something, spend money on something, and something costs money.

text: Could you _____ an eye on my bag while I go and buy a coffee?
note: Keep an eye on = watch something so it stays safe. A fixed phrase.

text: It isn't easy to _____ a living as a freelance designer.
note: Earn a living (or make a living) = get the money you need to live. You win a prize and gain experience.

text: All restaurants must _____ with the new hygiene regulations by March.
note: Comply with a rule = do what it says. Obey, follow and respect take a direct object, with no "with": obey the regulations.

text: The company was found to be in _____ of its contract and had to pay compensation.
note: In breach of a contract, rule or law = breaking it. Fracture and crack are physical breaks; an offence is a crime (you commit an offence).

text: We made it clear from the _____ that the project would take at least two years.
note: From the outset = from the very beginning. An origin or source is where something comes from; an outbreak is the sudden start of something bad (a war, a disease).

text: Refunds are only given at the manager's _____.
note: At someone's discretion = if they decide to, using their own judgement. A fixed phrase: we say "it's the manager's decision", but not "at the manager's decision".

text: Against all the _____, the small village team won the cup.
note: Against all (the) odds = although it seemed very unlikely. A fixed phrase; the other words don't go with "against all".

text: The government's spending plans have come under close _____ from the press.
note: Come under scrutiny = be examined carefully, often critically. We pay close attention to something, but nothing "comes under attention".

text: A momentary _____ of concentration caused the driver to miss the red light.
note: A lapse of concentration (or memory) = a short time when it fails. A gap is a space between things; a fault is a mistake or defect, not a moment.

text: At the age of 80, he finally agreed to _____ control of the company to his daughter.
note: Relinquish control or power = give it up, often unwillingly. You resign from a job and retire from work; neither takes "control" as an object.

text: The _____ of the work was done by volunteers.
note: The bulk of = most of. Volume, size and weight are measurements; "the volume of work" means how much work there is, not most of it.

text: The resort _____ mainly for families with young children.
note: Cater for (American: cater to) = provide what a group of people needs. Serves and supplies take an object with no "for"; attend to means deal with.

text: She quickly built up a good _____ with her students.
note: A rapport = a friendly relationship where people understand each other. Careful: a report is a written account (Spanish reporte), and in English we'd say a good relationship, not "a good relation".

text: The concert was a _____ to the band's late singer.
note: A tribute to someone = something that shows respect and admiration for them. We say in memory of and out of respect for; praise is uncountable (not "a praise").

text: The fact that the bridge is still standing is a _____ to the skill of its builders.
note: Be a testament to = clearly show how good something is. We say proof of, a sign of, and evidence is uncountable (not "an evidence").

text: She has a very low pain _____, so she hates going to the dentist.
note: A pain threshold = the point at which you start to feel pain. Limit is close in meaning but doesn't make this compound; a border is between countries.

text: Unfortunately, the meeting _____ with my dentist's appointment, so I can't come.
note: Two events clash = they happen at the same time, so you can't go to both. Crash and collide are about vehicles hitting things.

text: There's no point _____ on past mistakes: learn from them and move on.
note: Dwell on something = keep thinking or talking about it, usually something bad. The others are about being in a place and don't take "on" like this.

text: The company is about to _____ on an ambitious expansion plan.
note: Embark on something = start something new and important. We board a plane, enter a room and launch a plan (no "on").

text: Most students _____ for the online version of the course.
note: Opt for = choose. Choose, select and prefer take the thing directly, with no "for": most students choose the online version.

text: She felt lonely because she had no one to _____ in.
note: Confide in someone = tell them your secrets or private feelings. We count on and depend on someone; share takes "with".

text: Her first novel won critical _____ and quickly became a bestseller.
note: Critical acclaim = praise from critics (win / receive critical acclaim). Applause is clapping; fame is being well known, not praise from critics.

text: The new bypass should help to _____ traffic congestion in the town centre.
note: Alleviate = make a problem or suffering less bad. Soothe and comfort are for people or pain; heal is for wounds and illnesses.

text: The new law comes into _____ on 1 January.
note: Come into force = start to apply (also come into effect). A party or politician comes into power; we put a plan into practice, not a law.

text: It goes without _____ that you should back up your files regularly.
note: It goes without saying = it is obvious. A fixed phrase: always saying.

text: When the interviewer asked about her weaknesses, she was at a _____ for words.
note: Be at a loss for words = not know what to say. A fixed phrase; we say a lack of words, not "at a lack".

text: His argument doesn't hold _____: the figures he quotes are ten years old.
note: Not hold water = not be believable when you look at it closely. An idiom; we say it doesn't make sense, not "hold sense".

text: I wasn't sure he was telling the truth, but I gave him the _____ of the doubt.
note: Give someone the benefit of the doubt = believe them, although you're not sure. A fixed phrase.

text: Online banking was still in its _____ when I opened my first account.
note: In its infancy = at a very early stage of development. Childhood and youth are only used for people this way.

text: The rule applies to all staff, without _____.
note: Without exception = every one, with none left out. A fixed phrase.

text: Something is wrong with this essay, but I can't quite _____ my finger on it.
note: Can't put your finger on something = can't say exactly what it is. An idiom: always put.

text: I didn't mean to say her name instead of yours: it was a slip of the _____.
note: A slip of the tongue = a small mistake when speaking. A fixed phrase.

text: The judge stressed that her ruling did not create a legal _____ for similar cases.
note: A precedent = an earlier decision used as a guide for later ones; set or create a legal precedent. An example or instance is just one case of something; a sample is a small part used for testing.

text: After two days of discussion, the jury returned a _____ of not guilty.
note: A jury returns or reaches a verdict (guilty or not guilty). A judgement is given by a judge, and a sentence is the punishment that follows a guilty verdict.

text: Drivers who park here without a permit are _____ to a fine of up to £100.
note: Liable to a fine, a tax or a penalty = legally having to pay it. Likely and apt are followed by a verb (likely to rain); prone to is used for bad things that happen often (prone to injury).

text: I'm _____ to agree with you, although I'd like to see the figures first.
note: I'm inclined to agree = I think I agree, but not strongly. Prone and liable are about bad things that tend to happen; we say leaning towards, not leaning to agree.

text: With its narrow streets and old wooden houses, the village is _____ of a film set.
note: Reminiscent of = making you think of something. Similar takes "to", alike comes after the things compared (they are alike), and resembling takes no preposition.

text: Some parents _____ a lot of pressure on their children to do well at school.
note: Exert pressure or influence on someone (put pressure on also works). Force, press and make don't go with pressure in this way.

text: He was dismissed on the _____ that he had repeatedly broken company rules.
note: On the grounds that / on the grounds of = for this reason, usually an official one. We say for the reason that, not on the reasons that.

text: The new parking charges have become a bone of _____ between residents and the council.
note: A bone of contention = a subject people keep arguing about. A fixed phrase: no other noun works here.

text: If you don't choose a language, the app will use English by _____.
note: By default = automatically, unless you choose something else. Standard and normal are adjectives or nouns that don't follow "by" (as standard, as normal).

text: Let's _____ with the formalities: please call me Anna.
note: Dispense with = do without something you don't need. Dispose takes "of" (dispose of rubbish); discard and omit take a direct object.

text: Last year the university _____ an honorary degree on the novelist.
note: Confer something on someone = formally give an honour or a right. Award and grant take "to" (awarded a degree to her); present takes "with" or "to".

text: The region is in the _____ of the worst drought for fifty years.
note: In the grip of = strongly affected by something bad (a drought, a crisis, fear). Hold, clasp and handle are only about holding things with your hands.

text: Traffic in the city centre ground to a _____ after the accident.
note: Grind to a halt = slowly stop completely. Also come to a halt. We don't say ground to a pause, break or rest.

text: Although years have passed, she still _____ to the hope that her son is alive.
note: Cling to a hope or belief = refuse to give it up. Grip takes a direct object; keep and attach don't go with hope in this way.

text: In the _____ of the earthquake, thousands of families had nowhere to live.
note: In the aftermath of = in the period after a bad event. We say as a consequence of or as a result of, not in the.

text: She is a scientist first and _____, and a writer second.
note: First and foremost = most importantly. A fixed phrase. Utmost means greatest (of the utmost importance); uppermost means highest.

text: The suspect was taken into _____ shortly after the robbery.
note: Take someone into custody = arrest and keep them. We say put under arrest or put in jail, not taken into.

text: He was released on _____ and must report to the police every week until the trial.
note: Released on bail = let out before a trial after money is paid as a promise to return. Bond, deposit and guarantee don't follow released on.

text: The long working hours are starting to take their _____ on her health.
note: Take a or its toll on = cause damage over time. Cost, charge and fee are about money and don't fit this phrase.

text: Any costs _____ during the business trip will be paid back by the company.
note: Incur costs, debts or a fine = become responsible for paying them. Undergo and endure go with difficult experiences; contract goes with illnesses or debts, but not costs.

text: We hadn't planned a holiday: we booked the flights on the _____ of the moment.
note: On the spur of the moment = suddenly, without planning. A fixed phrase. Compare in the heat of the moment (when angry or excited).

text: The new rules will take _____ on 1 January.
note: Take effect = start to apply (also come into force). Take action means do something; power and practice don't go with take here.

text: Ladies and gentlemen, I'd like to _____ a toast to the bride and groom.
note: Propose a toast = ask everyone to drink to someone (raise a toast also works). Offer, suggest and present don't go with toast.

text: I don't know how long the meeting will last, so let's play it by _____.
note: Play it by ear = decide what to do as things happen, without a plan. A fixed phrase (learn something by heart is different).

text: Don't worry: in the _____ of time, you'll understand why we made this decision.
note: In the fullness of time = eventually, when the time is right. A fixed phrase.

text: You can't judge a whole country on the _____ of one short visit.
note: On the strength of = because of, based on. A fixed phrase (on the basis of means the same).

text: Her latest novel is head and _____ above anything she has written before.
note: Head and shoulders above = much better than. A fixed phrase.

text: The museum will remain closed until further _____.
note: Until further notice = until you are told something different. A fixed phrase used in official announcements.

text: As a rule of _____, allow one hour of study for every hour of class.
note: A rule of thumb = a practical guide based on experience, not an exact rule. A fixed phrase.

text: The new manager was given a _____ hand to run the department as she wished.
note: Give someone a free hand = let them do things their own way. Open hand and loose hand don't have this meaning.

text: With _____, it's easy to see where we went wrong.
note: With hindsight (or in hindsight) = looking back, knowing what you know now. We say in retrospect, not "with retrospect"; foresight is the opposite, seeing what will happen.

text: They hoped to settle the dispute without _____ to the courts.
note: Recourse to = using something as a way to get help, especially legal help. Don't mix it up with resource (something useful you have).

text: Several shops in the _____ of the station were damaged in the fire.
note: In the vicinity of = near. Surroundings take no "of" this way (the station's surroundings); a town has outskirts, a station doesn't.

text: After years of planning, the project finally came to _____.
note: Come to fruition = succeed after a long time of work. Plans bear fruit (not "come to fruit").

text: Despite our worries, the wedding went off without a _____.
note: Go off without a hitch = happen with no problems at all. A fixed phrase.

text: Salary will be _____ with experience.
note: Commensurate with = right in size or amount for something. The others take "to": proportional to, equal to, corresponding to.

text: I'm not _____ to the occasional glass of wine.
note: Not averse to = quite happy to have or do something (humorous understatement). Adverse means harmful (adverse effects); reluctant and unwilling are followed by to + verb.

text: All members must _____ to the club's code of conduct.
note: Adhere to a rule = follow it exactly. Obey and follow take no "to"; we comply with a rule.

text: The ugly new car park _____ from the beauty of the old town.
note: Detract from = make something seem less good. Distract means take someone's attention away; subtract and deduct are about numbers and money.

text: A goal in the last minute _____ the title for the home team.
note: Clinch a title, deal or victory = finally win it. Don't confuse it with clench (your fists or teeth).

text: The interviews have been recorded and preserved for _____.
note: For posterity = for people in the future. Heritage, ancestry and inheritance look back to the past.

text: As a child, she put her father on a _____ and couldn't see his faults.
note: Put someone on a pedestal = admire them so much that you think they are perfect. An idiom: always pedestal.

text: They got married after a _____ romance of just six weeks.
note: A whirlwind romance = one that happens very fast. Only whirlwind is used this way (also a whirlwind tour).

text: Critics say the court's ruling will open the _____ to thousands of similar claims.
note: Open the floodgates = suddenly let a lot of something happen. An idiom.

text: She has been at the _____ of the company for twenty years.
note: At the helm = in charge (a helm steers a ship). We'd also say at the head of, but not "at the steering" or "at the rudder".

text: Relations between the two countries are at a low _____.
note: At a low ebb = in a bad state (the ebb is when the sea goes out). We say at low tide (no "a"), and not about relations.

text: Tickets for the final were well _____ impossible to get.
note: Well nigh = almost (formal or literary). A fixed phrase; we say almost impossible or nearly impossible, but not "well near".

text: Farmers struggle to _____ out a living from the poor soil.
note: Eke out a living = get just enough to live on, with difficulty. We earn a living and scrape a living, both without "out".

text: I need some time to _____ it over before I make a decision.
note: Mull something over = think about it carefully for a while. Ponder and consider take no "over"; we reflect on something.

text: In _____ to her wishes, the funeral was a private one.
note: In deference to someone's wishes = because you respect them. A fixed phrase; the others don't go with "in … to".

text: The politician complained that her comments had been taken out of _____.
note: Take something out of context = repeat only part of it, so its meaning changes. A fixed phrase.

text: The two leaders are at _____ over the issue of trade.
note: Be at loggerheads (with someone) = disagree strongly. We say at a crossroads (a point of decision), at daggers drawn and cross swords.

text: She was on _____ all week, waiting to hear whether she'd got the job.
note: On tenterhooks = nervous while waiting for news. Also on pins and needles, but never on needles alone.

text: By the time the vote was held, the result was a foregone _____.
note: A foregone conclusion = a result that is certain before it happens. A fixed phrase.

text: The deal was rescued at the eleventh _____, just before the deadline.
note: At the eleventh hour = at the last possible moment. We say at the last minute or moment, but the idiom uses eleventh hour.

text: The company pays lip _____ to equality but has no women on its board.
note: Pay lip service to = say you support something without doing anything about it. We pay attention and pay tribute, but the idiom is lip service.

text: After years of not speaking, the brothers decided to bury the _____.
note: Bury the hatchet = stop arguing and become friends again. An idiom: always hatchet.

text: She made no _____ of her dislike for her new boss.
note: Make no secret of = not try to hide something. A fixed phrase.

text: His rude remarks at the dinner were completely beyond the _____.
note: Beyond the pale = completely unacceptable. An old idiom (a pale was a fence), but today only pale is used.

text: Halfway through the year, it's time to take _____ of what we've achieved.
note: Take stock (of) = think carefully about a situation before deciding what to do. A fixed phrase.
